```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

This tutorial shows you how to build a prediction model and, above all,
how to find out **how well it will really work in new patients**. You do
not need any previous knowledge of machine learning, and very little of
R.

This is the first of four tutorials:

1.  **Get started** (this tutorial, about 30–40 minutes): building a
    model and estimating its accuracy correctly.
2.  [Evaluating and interpreting your model](evaluating-and-interpreting.html)
    (about 20–30 minutes): discrimination, calibration, relevant variables,
    and predicting new patients.
3.  [Missing data](missing-data.html) (about 20–30 minutes): multiple
    imputation.
4.  [Continuous and survival outcomes, regression to the mean, and multisite data](other-outcomes-and-sites.html)
    (about 30–40 minutes).

We recommend following all of them in order, but feel free to go directly
to the one you need.

In this tutorial, you will learn to:

1.  Fit a prediction model with `glmnet_fit` and apply it with
    `glmnet_predict` (or just `predict`).
2.  Understand why evaluating a model with the same patients used to
    build it gives results that are too good to be true.
3.  Estimate the accuracy of a model correctly with `cv`
    (cross-validation).
4.  Include categorical variables with `data.frame2glmnet.matrix`.

All the code runs in a few seconds, so we encourage you to run it
yourself as you read.


## New to R?

If you have used R before, you can skip this section.

**Installing.** Install R from <https://cran.r-project.org> and, if you
want a friendlier interface, RStudio from <https://posit.co>. Then
install this package by typing the following in the R console (you only
need to do this once):

```{r, eval = FALSE}
install.packages("easy.glmnet")
```

Every time you open R, load the package with:

```{r}
library(easy.glmnet)
```

**Objects.** R stores values in objects with `=` (you may also see `<-`,
which does the same). Typing the name of an object shows its value:

```{r}
a = 5
a * 2
```

**Vectors** are lists of values, created with `c()`:

```{r}
ages = c(34, 51, 28)
mean(ages)
```

**Data frames** are tables, where each row is an observation (e.g., a
patient) and each column is a variable. You can get a column with `$`,
and select rows and columns with `[rows, columns]`:

```{r}
df = data.frame(age = c(34, 51, 28), sex = c("F", "M", "F"))
df$age
df[1:2, ]       # rows 1 and 2, all columns
df[, "sex"]     # all rows, column "sex"
```

**Functions** take some inputs (arguments) and return an output. You can
write your own with `function`. The last line is what the function
returns:

```{r}
add_ten = function (x) {
  x + 10
}
add_ten(5)
```

This is important because, as you will see, to cross-validate a model
you will write two small functions.

Finally, to get help about any function, type `?` followed by its name,
e.g., `?mean` or `?glmnet_fit`.


## The data

The package includes two simulated datasets:

-   `patients`: 100 patients who were followed to see whether they
    relapsed. For each patient, we have 40 numeric variables (`X1` to
    `X40`), 3 categorical variables (`C1` to `C3`), and whether they
    relapsed (`relapse`: 1 = yes, 0 = no).
-   `new_patients`: 900 other patients from the same population.

```{r}
dim(patients)                 # number of rows (patients) and columns
patients[1:5, c(1:3, 41:47)]  # first 5 patients, some of the columns
table(patients$relapse)       # how many relapsed
```

Our goal is to use the data of the 100 patients to build a model that
predicts relapse in future patients (`new_patients`), and to know how accurate these
predictions will be.

In a real study, you would not have `new_patients`: future patients have
not arrived yet! Here we have them because the data are simulated, and
we will use them as a "crystal ball" to check which methods tell us the
truth about the accuracy of our models.


## Step 1: A first prediction model

### Preparing the data

Most prediction functions need the predictors as a numeric **matrix** (a
table with only numbers) and the outcome as a **vector** (a single row or column of elements). Let's start
with the 40 numeric variables:

```{r}
x = as.matrix(patients[, 1:40])  # columns X1, X2, ..., X40
y = patients$relapse
x_new = as.matrix(new_patients[, 1:40])
y_new = new_patients$relapse
```

Some steps of this tutorial involve randomness. To obtain exactly the
same results as shown here, we fix the "seed" of the random number
generator:

```{r}
set.seed(1)
```

### A standard logistic regression

Many researchers would start with a standard logistic regression
including all the variables:

```{r}
m_glm = glm(y ~ ., data = data.frame(x), family = "binomial")
```

R warns us that the fitted probabilities are 0 or 1. Keep this in mind,
it is a first sign of trouble. Let's see how well the model predicts
relapse in our patients. The function `predict` returns, for each
patient, the probability of relapse, and `round` converts it into a
prediction: 1 (relapse) if the probability is higher than 0.5, or 0 (no
relapse) otherwise:

```{r}
y.pred = round(predict(m_glm, type = "response"))
simple.accuracy(y, y.pred, "bac")
```

`simple.accuracy` compares the actual outcomes (`y`) with the
predictions (`y.pred`). Here, it returns three numbers, each with the lower
(.lwr) and upper (.upr) limits of its 95% confidence interval:

-   `se` (sensitivity): the proportion of patients who relapsed that the
    model correctly predicted would relapse. 1 (i.e., 100%) means that
    the model correctly predicted all the patients who relapsed.
-   `sp` (specificity): the proportion of patients who did not relapse
    that the model correctly predicted would not relapse. 1 (i.e., 100%)
    means that the model correctly predicted all the patients who did
    not relapse.
-   `bac` (balanced accuracy): the mean of the two.

A perfect model! Too good to be true? Let's use our crystal ball and
apply the model to the new patients:

```{r}
y_new.pred = round(predict(m_glm, data.frame(x_new), type = "response"))
simple.accuracy(y_new, y_new.pred, "bac")
```

In new patients, the balanced accuracy drops quite a bit. What happened?

The model has **memorized** the 100 patients instead of learning general
rules. With 40 variables and only 100 patients, the model can adjust to
the random particularities of most or all patients, which will not be
repeated in new patients. This is called **overfitting**. It is like a
student who memorizes the answers of a mock exam: they get a perfect
score in that exam, but not in the real one.

### A lasso model

A lasso model is a type of regression designed to reduce overfitting: it
makes the coefficients smaller ("shrinks" them) and can remove the
variables that do not seem useful. `glmnet_fit` fits a lasso model in
one line  (Solanes et al., 2022):

```{r}
m_lasso = glmnet_fit(x, y, family = "binomial")
```

(If you see a warning about `type.measure`, it only informs users of
previous versions of the package that a default setting has changed; you
can ignore it.)

To apply it to some patients, use `glmnet_predict` (or just `predict`), which
returns the probabilities of relapse:

```{r}
y.pred = round(predict(m_lasso, x))
simple.accuracy(y, y.pred, "bac")
```

Again, in the same patients used to build the model, the balanced
accuracy is very high . Let's look at the new patients:

```{r}
y_new.pred = round(predict(m_lasso, x_new))
simple.accuracy(y_new, y_new.pred, "bac")
```

The lasso model may work some better than the standard logistic regression in
new patients, but its accuracy is still much lower than it seemed. Thus,
whatever the method (Radua & Koutsouleris, 2024):

> **Lesson 1: Never evaluate a model with the same patients that you
> used to build it.**

But in a real study, we have no crystal ball. How can we know the
accuracy of a model in new patients if we only have the patients used to
build it? The answer is cross-validation.


## Step 2: Cross-validation

### The idea

Cross-validation splits the patients into several groups called
**folds** (usually 10). Then, for each fold:

1.  It builds a model using the patients of all the other folds (the
    **training** set).
2.  It applies this model to the patients of this fold (the **test**
    set).

```         
         Fold 1   Fold 2   Fold 3   ...   Fold 10
Round 1:  test    train    train    ...    train
Round 2:  train   test     train    ...    train
Round 3:  train   train    test     ...    train
...
Round 10: train   train    train    ...    test
```

At the end, each patient has a prediction from a model that never saw
them, just like a new patient. Comparing these predictions with the
actual outcomes tells us how well the model works in "new" patients.

### Doing it with `cv`

The function `cv` does all the work (dividing the patients into folds,
building the models, applying them, and collecting the predictions), but
it needs you to tell it two things, as two small functions:

-   `fit_fun`: how to build a model from the training set. It receives
    the predictors and outcomes of the training set and must return the
    model.
-   `predict_fun`: how to apply a model to the test set. It receives the
    model and the predictors of the test set and must return the
    predictions.

```{r}
fit_fun = function (x_training, y_training) {
  glmnet_fit(x_training, y_training, family = "binomial")
}
predict_fun = function (m, x_test) {
  round(predict(m, x_test))
}
```

Note that these functions do exactly what we did before with `glmnet_fit` and
`glmnet_predict` (or just `predict`), but with the training and test sets
of each fold. Now we can run the cross-validation:

```{r}
res = cv(x, y, family = "binomial", fit_fun, predict_fun, verbose = FALSE)
```

`res$predictions` contains, for each patient, the fold, the actual
outcome and the prediction:

```{r}
head(res$predictions)
```

Let's see the accuracy (we just have to print the `cv` object):

```{r}
res
```

The cross-validation estimates a balanced accuracy very close to the one that
the lasso model actually achieved in the new patients. Unlike the evaluation
with the same patients, the cross-validation tells the truth, even without a
crystal ball.

### A note on randomness

`cv` assigns the patients to the folds randomly (though ensuring that
each fold has a similar proportion of patients who relapsed). With
another seed, the folds would be different, and the estimate would
change a bit, especially in small samples like this one. This is why we
used `set.seed`: to make the results reproducible.


## Step 3: Data leakage

### Cross-validation can also be optimistic if used wrongly

Imagine that, before the cross-validation, we select the variables with
the lasso model that we fitted in Step 1 with all the patients (`m_lasso`; recall that the lasso sets some
coefficients exactly to zero, so it uses only some of the variables), and then
we cross-validate a model that uses only these variables. It seems
reasonable: we only keep the variables that seem useful. Let's try:

```{r}
selected = names(m_lasso$beta)  # variables selected by the lasso of Step 1
res = cv(x[, selected], y, family = "binomial", fit_fun, predict_fun, verbose = FALSE)
res
```

The cross-validation estimates a higher balanced accuracy than in step 2! But
let's use our crystal ball: we build the model with these variables and all the
patients, and apply it to the new patients:

```{r}
m_leak = glmnet_fit(x[, selected], y, family = "binomial")
y_new.pred = round(predict(m_leak, x_new[, selected]))
simple.accuracy(y_new, c(y_new.pred), "bac")
```

Quite less. The cross-validation was too optimistic. Why? Because the
variables were selected using all the patients, including those that
later played the role of test set! In other words, the selection "saw"
the test set, so these patients were no longer like new patients. This
is called **data leakage**: information from the test set leaks into the
models.

### The solution

There is a simple solution (Radua & Koutsouleris, 2024):

> **Lesson 2: Every step that learns something from the data is part of
> the model. Thus, it must be inside `fit_fun`, and must use only the
> training set.**


## Step 4: Categorical variables

So far, we have only used the numeric variables. But our patients also
have three categorical variables (`C1`, `C2`, and `C3`), with values
`A`, `B`, or `C`. `glmnet_fit` needs a numeric matrix, so we must first
convert each categorical variable into several numeric variables (called
"dummy" variables), one for each value. `data.frame2glmnet.matrix` does
it for you:

```{r}
df = patients[, 1:43] # all predictors
df2mat = data.frame2glmnet.matrix_fit(df)
x_all = data.frame2glmnet.matrix(df2mat, df)
x_all[1:5, 41:49]
```

For example, `C1:A` is 1 if the patient has `C1 = A`, and 0 otherwise.

Note that there are two functions. `data.frame2glmnet.matrix_fit`
**learns** how to convert the data (which variables are categorical,
which values they can take, etc.), and `data.frame2glmnet.matrix`
**applies** this conversion to some data. Following Lesson 2, the
conversion must be learned inside `fit_fun`, using only the training
set. Converting the data learns much less than selecting variables, but
it is a good habit, and other steps learn a lot (e.g., imputing missing
values, as you will see in a subsequent tutorial).

So, the model now has two parts: the conversion and the lasso. `fit_fun`
can return both in a `list`, and `predict_fun` can then use both:

```{r}
fit_fun = function (df_training, y_training) {
  df2mat = data.frame2glmnet.matrix_fit(df_training)
  x_training = data.frame2glmnet.matrix(df2mat, df_training)
  list(
    df2mat = df2mat,
    lasso = glmnet_fit(x_training, y_training, family = "binomial")
  )
}
predict_fun = function (m, df_test) {
  x_test = data.frame2glmnet.matrix(m$df2mat, df_test)
  round(predict(m$lasso, x_test))
}
df = patients[, 1:43] # all predictors
res = cv(df, y, family = "binomial", fit_fun, predict_fun, verbose = FALSE)
res
```

The results are the same as without the categorical variables because, in these data, they are unrelated to relapse, so the lasso does not select them.


## Summary

-   A model evaluated with the same patients used to build it looks much
    better than it is (**Lesson 1**).
-   Cross-validation (`cv`) estimates how well the model will work in
    new patients. You only need to write `fit_fun` (how to build the
    model) and `predict_fun` (how to apply it).
-   Categorical variables can be converted into numeric variables using
    `data.frame2glmnet.matrix`.
-   Every step that learns from the data, such as selecting variables or
    even converting categorical variables, is part of the model and goes
    inside `fit_fun`. Otherwise, the cross-validation will be too
    optimistic (**Lesson 2**).

Both lessons are part of rule 4 of the ten simple rules for using
machine learning in mental health research (Radua & Koutsouleris, 2024),
which apply to other fields too. We recommend reading them all.

In the next tutorial, [Evaluating and interpreting your model](evaluating-and-interpreting.html)
(`vignette("evaluating-and-interpreting")`), you will learn other ways to measure
accuracy and how to interpret your models.
